fields.title: What job the product is hired for
fields.keyTakeaway: Look at what a person does instead of using your product—that is where the real job is visible. A competitor is almost never who you think it is.
fields.checkQuestion: Business owners manage the schedule in a messaging app. What job did they hire the messaging app for?
fields.blocks/0/text: The key question of this node: **how does the customer solve their problems right now?** Not “what do they want,” but what they actually do today, before you.
fields.blocks/1/text: **What happens if you ignore this question.** The product gets compared feature-by-feature with similar products, missing that the real alternative is a notepad, a messenger, or an assistant who “just remembers.”
fields.blocks/2/title: The job a product is hired for
fields.blocks/2/items/0: **What was the person doing before they started doing this?** The previous solution is the competitor.
fields.blocks/2/items/1: **At what point did they decide they couldn’t go on like this?** A trigger event, not gradual dissatisfaction.
fields.blocks/2/items/2: **What would have needed to happen for them to stay with the old way?** This reveals the retaining forces.
fields.blocks/2/items/3: A job is framed as the **progress** a person makes, not as a feature.
fields.blocks/3/text:
Business owners kept the schedule in a group chat. Formally, this is bad: there is no history, and you cannot find last week’s schedule.

But conversations showed what job it was hired for: **making sure the person saw it**. In a chat, you can see read receipts and follow up immediately.

A product with a pretty calendar did not do this job—which is why the chat stayed, even for those using Smena.

The takeaway was not about the calendar: they needed to show which employees opened the schedule.
fields.blocks/3/title: Smena: what the messenger was hired for
fields.blocks/4/text: Most often, it is a spreadsheet, paper, a messenger, or a human. None of these show up in competitor analysis if you search by product names.
fields.blocks/4/title: A competitor is what gets replaced, not what looks similar
fields.blocks/5/text: JTBD explains the past well and predicts the future poorly: by reconstructing the job, you will understand why the current solution is hired, but you will not know if they will hire yours. Also, the phrasing easily turns into a word game—if the job sounds like “becoming a better version of yourself,” you have strayed too far from what is observable.
